title: Fast Cooling, Slow Cooling
question: Why do some igneous rocks have big grains and others almost none?
hook: Whether molten rock hardens deep underground or out in the open decides what the finished rock looks like.
idea: Magma that cools slowly inside the crust grows coarse, visible grains, while lava that cools fast at the surface becomes fine-grained or glassy.

beats.prompt: Lava pours out of a fissure onto the ground and quickly turns solid. What will the new rock look like up close?

choices.label: Large crystals easy to spot by eye
choices.feedback: Big visible grains come from magma that cools slowly underground, not from fast-cooling lava.

choices.label: Layers of hardened sand and mud
choices.feedback: Layers of sediment make sedimentary rock, not cooled lava.

beats.explain: Magma brought to the surface solidifies rapidly, so extrusive rocks are fine-grained or even glassy.

beats.prompt: Sort each rock by where it formed
beats.explain: Granite, gabbro and diorite are common intrusive rocks, while basalt is the most common extrusive rock and tuff is made of explosively erupted material.

beats.prompt: Match each magma to how it typically behaves
pairs: Cinder cones of ash, tuff and lava
beats.explain: Basaltic magma behaves like thick oil, andesite can be as stiff as cold molasses, and rhyolite is up to 10,000 times as viscous as basalt, so each builds different features.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Magma rises because it is less dense than the rock it came from.
Some of it stops inside the crust, surrounded by country rock.
Country rock draws heat away quickly, so this magma cools fast.
That is why intrusive rocks have grains you can see by eye.
beats.explain: Country rock is an excellent thermal insulator, so trapped magma cools slowly, and slow cooling is what produces the coarse grains.
